topics.name: Process Structures
topics.summary: A process is a program in execution. From creation to completion it moves through states: new, ready, running, blocked (waiting), and terminated. The operating system keeps track of each process with a Process Control Block (PCB), and it keeps the ready processes in a ready list.
objectives: Describe the states a process moves through, from creation to termination.
Explain what a Process Control Block stores and why the OS needs it.
key_ideas: A newly created process enters the ready state and waits for the CPU.
A running process is one the scheduler has chosen. With one CPU, only one process runs at a time.
A blocked (waiting) process needs I/O, user input, or a locked critical region. It waits and does not use the CPU.
A terminated process has finished. Its PCB is deleted and its resources are released.
The PCB holds the process ID, its state, the program counter, CPU registers, scheduling priority, memory information, and I/O status.
The ready list is ordered by priority.
Dispatching gives the CPU to a selected process. A context switch saves the state of one process and loads the state of another.
topics.example: A program starts and enters the ready state. The scheduler picks it and it runs. It then asks to read a file, so it moves to blocked. When the read finishes it returns to ready, runs again, and finally terminates, and its PCB is deleted.

topics.name: Scheduling and Dispatching
topics.summary: The scheduler decides which process should run next and how the ready queue is kept in order. The dispatcher then removes that process from the ready queue and gives it the CPU. They are separate parts of the operating system.
objectives: Explain the difference between the scheduler and the dispatcher.
Compare preemptive and non-preemptive scheduling algorithms.
key_ideas: The scheduler puts processes in the ready queue and maintains it.
The dispatcher removes a process from the ready queue, sets up its state, and transfers control to it. The time this takes is the dispatch latency.
There are three kinds of scheduler: long-term (chooses batch jobs), medium-term (handles swapped-out processes), and short-term (picks from the ready processes in memory).
Preemptive algorithms, such as Round Robin, SRTF, and Priority, can take the CPU from a running process. Non-preemptive algorithms, such as FCFS and SJF, let it finish its CPU turn.
Goals: use the CPU and disks well, keep overhead low, reduce response time, and share the CPU fairly.
topics.example: Processes P1 to P4 arrive in that order and FIFO scheduling is used. The scheduler chooses P1 first and the dispatcher gives it the CPU. Then the same happens for P2, P3, and P4.

topics.name: Interrupts
topics.summary: An interrupt is a signal that tells the CPU to stop what it is doing and run part of the operating system. Interrupts are how the OS regains control from a running user process. Without them, a user program could keep the CPU for as long as it liked.
objectives: Explain what an interrupt is and why the OS needs interrupts.
Distinguish hardware interrupts, software interrupts, and traps.
key_ideas: Hardware interrupts come from devices, such as a key press or a finished disk operation.
Software interrupts are made by a program that wants a system call.
Traps are made by the CPU itself when an error happens, such as an illegal instruction or an addressing violation.
The timer interrupt makes sure the OS gets control regularly.
On a task switch caused by a timer interrupt, the context switcher first saves the state of the interrupted task, then sets up system code, then calls the dispatcher.
topics.example: A program is running when the timer interrupt fires. The OS saves the program's state, the dispatcher picks the next ready process, and that process runs.

topics.name: Concurrent Execution
topics.summary: Concurrent execution means several instruction sequences run at the same time, or appear to. Processes and threads communicate through shared memory or message passing. It makes systems faster and better at using resources, but it also causes problems such as deadlock and starvation.
objectives: Describe the advantages of running processes concurrently.
Explain the problems that concurrent execution creates.
key_ideas: Advantages: several applications run at once, resources unused by one application can be used by another, response and turnaround times improve, and throughput increases.
Problems: sharing global resources safely is hard, because the order of reads and writes matters. The OS must allocate resources well, and errors are hard to reproduce.
The relative speed of processes cannot be predicted. It depends on the other processes, how the OS handles interrupts, and the scheduling policy.
Drawbacks: applications must be protected from each other and coordinated, and switching between them adds overhead.
topics.example: Two processes each update the same global variable. Whether the final value is correct depends on the order in which their reads and writes happen. This is why concurrent execution needs coordination.

topics.name: Mutual Exclusion
topics.summary: When several processes share a resource, such as a variable, they must take turns using it. Mutual exclusion (MUTEX) guarantees that no two processes are in the critical section at the same time. The critical section is the part of the code that uses the shared resource.
objectives: Explain what mutual exclusion guarantees.
Describe what a race condition is and how mutual exclusion prevents it.
key_ideas: A race condition happens when shared data is accessed without coordination, and the result depends on the order of the accesses.
Example from the notes: a counter starts at 1, and two processes each add 1. The correct result is 3. Without coordination, one update can be lost and the result is 2.
A good mutual exclusion solution must be free of deadlock: if processes try to enter the critical section, one of them must eventually succeed.
topics.example: Two processes both want to update the same counter. Mutual exclusion makes one process finish its update before the other starts, so both increments are counted.

topics.name: Deadlock
topics.summary: Deadlock happens when a set of processes each wait for something that only another process in the set can provide, so none of them can continue. The notes say deadlock needs four conditions to hold at the same time. The OS can prevent it, avoid it, or detect it and recover.
objectives: List the four conditions needed for deadlock.
Compare the Wait-Die and Wound-Wait schemes.
key_ideas: The four conditions: mutual exclusion (a resource is held by one process at a time), hold and wait (a process holding resources can ask for more), no preemption (resources cannot be taken away), and circular wait (a chain of processes, each waiting for the next).
Prevention breaks one of the four conditions. Avoidance checks each request before granting it. The Banker's algorithm does this by checking whether the system stays in a safe state.
Wait-Die: an older process may wait for a younger one, but a younger process that asks for an older process's item dies (is restarted later).
Wound-Wait: an older process wounds a younger one (forces it to roll back and release the item), but a younger process waits for an older one.
A wait-for graph with a cycle means a deadlock is present.
topics.example: Process A holds resource X and waits for Y. Process B holds Y and waits for X. Neither can move forward. This is a circular wait, and it is a deadlock.

topics.name: Semaphores
topics.summary: A semaphore is an integer variable that controls access to shared resources. It is changed only by two operations, wait and signal. Wait decreases the value, if it is positive. Signal increases it.
objectives: Explain how the wait and signal operations change a semaphore.
key_ideas: wait(S) decreases S if S is positive. Otherwise the process must wait.
signal(S) increases S by one.
In the producer-consumer problem three semaphores are used: S for mutual exclusion (starts at 1), E for empty slots in the buffer (starts at n), and F for filled slots (starts at 0).
topics.example: A buffer has 5 slots, so E starts at 5 and F starts at 0. Before adding an item, the producer waits on E, so E goes down by one. Before removing an item, the consumer waits on F, so F goes down by one.

topics.name: Monitors
topics.summary: A monitor is a programming-language construct that bundles shared data, the procedures that use it, and the synchronization between calls. Condition variables let a thread wait inside a monitor until some condition becomes true.
objectives: Describe what a monitor provides.
Explain the role of condition variables in a monitor.
key_ideas: A monitor lets only one caller use the shared data at a time.
Condition variables let threads wait until a condition occurs. Operations 'wake one' and 'wake all' wake waiting threads.
Condition variables are user-mode objects and cannot be shared across processes.
A rendezvous happens when two processes synchronize and exchange messages.
topics.example: A consumer finds the buffer empty and waits on a condition variable. When a producer adds an item, it signals the variable, and the waiting consumer wakes up.

topics.name: Producer-Consumer Problem
topics.summary: One producer puts items into a shared fixed-size buffer and one consumer takes them out. This is also called the bounded-buffer problem. The buffer must not overflow or underflow, and the two processes must not access it at the same time.
objectives: Explain how semaphores S, E, and F solve the producer-consumer problem.
key_ideas: The producer produces only when the buffer is not full. If it is full, the producer sleeps.
The consumer consumes only when the buffer is not empty. If it is empty, the consumer sleeps.
The producer and consumer must not touch the buffer at the same time.
Producer: wait(E), wait(S), append, signal(S), signal(F).
Consumer: wait(F), wait(S), take, signal(S), signal(E).
topics.example: The producer adds 3 items to a 5-slot buffer, so E becomes 2 and F becomes 3. The consumer takes one item: it waits on F (F becomes 2), and then signals E (E becomes 3).

topics.name: Synchronization
topics.summary: Synchronization makes processes or threads wait for each other at the right points. A race condition happens when two threads access a shared variable at the same time, and the final value depends on which one writes last.
objectives: Explain how race conditions occur.
Explain how a barrier keeps processes in step.
key_ideas: In the example Total = Total + val1 and Total = Total - val2 running together, the value written last is kept and the other update is lost.
Some applications run in phases. A barrier at the end of each phase blocks each process until all processes have reached it.
A spinlock makes a thread loop, checking until the lock is free. It suits short waits on multiprocessor systems, but a thread that holds a lock for a long time makes others waste CPU time.
topics.example: Four workers finish phase 1. Each one waits at the barrier. When all four have arrived, phase 2 starts for all of them.

topics.name: Multiprocessor Issues
topics.summary: On a multiprocessor system, several CPUs run threads at the same time, so locks and reentrant code need special care. A spinlock is a lock that a thread waits for by looping until the lock becomes free.
objectives: Explain how a spinlock works.
Explain when a spinlock is suitable and when it is not.
key_ideas: A spinlock suits short waits on multiprocessors. The waiting thread stays active, so no context switch is needed.
The problems with spinlocks: if a thread holds the lock for a long time, other threads waste CPU time, and an unfair lock can leave a waiting thread starved.
A reentrant procedure can be interrupted in the middle and called again safely, or run on several processors at once.
A non-reentrant spinlock makes a thread that takes it a second time wait forever for itself.
topics.example: Thread A takes a spinlock to update a shared list for a moment. Thread B, on another CPU, keeps checking the lock in a loop until A releases it, and then takes it.

topics.name: Partitioning
topics.summary: In partitioned memory, main memory is divided into partitions, and each partition holds one process. As processes come and go, the free memory breaks into pieces. This is called fragmentation.
objectives: Distinguish internal fragmentation from external fragmentation.
Explain how compaction reduces external fragmentation.
key_ideas: Internal fragmentation: a block given to a process is bigger than the process, so some of the block is unused.
External fragmentation: the total free memory is enough for a request, but it is not in one contiguous block.
Compaction moves memory contents so the free memory is in one block. It needs dynamic relocation to work.
Placement policies (best fit, first fit, worst fit) decide which free partition a process gets.
topics.example: A process needing 3 MB is placed in a 5 MB partition. The 2 MB left over inside that partition is wasted. This is internal fragmentation.

topics.name: Swapping
topics.summary: Swapping moves a whole process out of main memory to disk, and later brings it back. It lets the system run more processes than fit in memory at once, and it increases the number of processes sharing the CPU.
objectives: Explain how swapping moves processes between memory and disk.
Describe the time cost of swapping a process.
key_ideas: Swapping out sends a process to secondary memory. Swapping in returns it to main memory when space is free.
Swapping takes time. The total includes moving the process out, moving it back in, and the time the process needs to regain memory.

Low memory holds the operating system and high memory holds user processes. Single-partition allocation uses a relocation register and a limit register to protect processes. Multiple-partition allocation gives each process one fixed-size partition.
topics.example: A 2048 KB process is swapped out to disk at about 1 MB per second, which takes about 2 seconds. Swapping it back in takes another 2 seconds, so the total is about 4 seconds, before other overheads.

topics.name: Paging
topics.summary: Paging divides a process's address space into fixed-size pages, and physical memory into frames of the same size. A page table maps each page to a frame, so a page can go into any free frame. This avoids external fragmentation and is the basis of virtual memory.
objectives: Explain how a page table maps pages to frames.
Convert a logical address into a physical address.
key_ideas: A logical address is a page number plus an offset. A physical address is a frame number plus the same offset.
The page table records which frame holds each page.
Demand paging loads a page only when it is referenced. Referencing a page that is not in memory causes a page fault.
Page replacement policies (FIFO, LRU, LFU) are covered in their own topic.
Paging still causes internal fragmentation, and the page table needs memory of its own.
topics.example: The page table starts at address 4096 and the page number is 128, so the entry is at 4096 + 128 = 4224. If page 128 is in memory at address 65,536 and the word offset is 32, the physical address is 65,536 + 32 = 65,568.

topics.name: Segmentation
topics.summary: Segmentation divides a program into segments of different sizes, usually one per logical part such as a function or a data structure. Unlike pages, segments are variable in length. Many systems combine segmentation with paging.
objectives: Compare segments with pages.
Describe what the segment map table stores.
key_ideas: A segment map table stores, for each segment, its starting address and its length.
A logical address is a segment number and an offset within the segment.
In the combined approach, segments are used from the programmer's point of view, but each segment is split into fixed-size pages for allocation.
Virtual memory can be built with demand paging or demand segmentation. It lets a program be larger than physical memory.
topics.example: A program has a segment for its main function, a segment for its utility functions, and a segment for its data. Each segment is a different size.

topics.name: Page Replacement Policies
topics.summary: When a page fault happens and no free frame is left, the OS must choose a page to replace. A good replacement algorithm causes few page faults. The notes compare algorithms by running them on a reference string and counting the faults.
objectives: Apply FIFO, LRU, and LFU to a reference string and count the page faults.
Explain why OPT is used as a benchmark.
key_ideas: A reference string is the sequence of page numbers a program uses. A repeated reference to a page that is already in memory does not cause a fault.
FIFO replaces the oldest page in memory. It is easy to implement.
LRU replaces the page that has not been used for the longest time.
LFU replaces the page with the smallest count. Its weakness is that a page used heavily at the start, and never again, stays in memory.
MFU replaces the page with the largest count, on the argument that the page with the smallest count was probably just brought in.
OPT replaces the page that will not be used for the longest time. It has the fewest faults but needs knowledge of the future, so it serves as a benchmark.
The clock algorithm approximates LRU using a use bit for each frame.
topics.example: For the reference string 1, 3, 0, 3, 5, 6, 3 with 3 frames, FIFO gives 6 page faults in the notes' example.

topics.name: Overlays
topics.summary: Overlaying lets a program run when there is not enough physical memory for all of it. The program is split into pieces, called overlays, that share the same logical addresses. Only one piece is in memory at a time.
objectives: Explain how overlaying lets a program run in less memory.
Describe the main drawback of overlays.
key_ideas: The programmer defines two or more overlay segments so that no two of them need to be in memory at the same time.
The OS manages the swapping of overlay segments in and out of memory.
The main disadvantage is that the programmer must plan the overlays in detail, which takes a lot of work.
topics.example: A program has a setup part and a calculation part that are never needed at the same time. The calculation overlay is loaded into the same memory area that the setup overlay used.

topics.name: Placement Policies
topics.summary: When a process needs memory, the system must choose a free partition for it. The notes describe best fit, first fit, worst fit, and the buddy system.
objectives: Compare best fit, first fit, and worst fit placement.
Explain how the buddy system chooses a block.
key_ideas: Best fit picks the smallest hole that is large enough. It uses memory well but is slower, and it can leave tiny useless holes.
First fit picks the first hole that is large enough. It is the fastest, but the leftover space can be wasted.
Worst fit always picks the largest hole, so the leftover piece is large enough to be useful.
The buddy system keeps block sizes as powers of 2 and splits blocks in halves until one fits. It is fast, but rounding up to a power of 2 wastes memory.
topics.example: A 70 KB process is placed in a 512 KB memory using the buddy system. The 512 KB block is split into two 256 KB halves, one 256 KB half is split into two 128 KB blocks, and one 128 KB block is given to the process.

topics.name: Caching
topics.summary: A cache is a small amount of fast memory that holds copies of data used often. A cache hit means the data is found in the cache. A cache miss means it has to be fetched from slower memory. Caching is one of the most effective ways to speed up memory access.
objectives: Calculate effective access time using the hit ratio.
Explain what a cache hit and a cache miss are.
key_ideas: The hit ratio H is the share of accesses that find their data in the cache. A good cache controller reaches 95 percent or more.
Effective access time: EAT = h x tmem + (1 - h) x tdisk, where h is the fraction of references that do not cause a page fault.
Speed-up: S = tm / (H x tc + (1 - H) x tm), where tm is memory access time and tc is cache access time.
The kernel also caches device data, for example in its I/O subsystem.
topics.example: If 95 out of every 100 accesses hit the cache, most accesses are fast. The few misses still matter, because each one is much slower and they can noticeably raise the average time.

topics.name: Thrashing
topics.summary: Thrashing is when a system spends most of its time moving pages between disk and memory and very little time doing useful work. It happens when the processes need more memory than the system has.
objectives: Explain what causes thrashing.
Describe how working sets help prevent thrashing.
key_ideas: The notes' example: many users reference 50 pages, but memory has 40. Each page brought in forces out a page that will soon be needed, so the system keeps reading and writing.
Thrashing happens because the system does not know when it has taken on more work than it can handle.
Fixes: work out how much memory each process needs, and change scheduling so that only groups of processes whose needs fit run together.
If one process alone is too big for memory, the OS cannot fix it.
The clock algorithm approximates LRU using use bits, and it helps decide which pages to replace.
topics.example: Fifty pages are referenced by active processes, but only 40 frames exist. Every new page fault evicts a page that is needed a moment later, so the system spends its time swapping pages rather than running programs.

topics.name: Working Sets
topics.summary: A process's working set is the collection of pages it has been using recently. The working set must be in memory, or the process will thrash. The idea was proposed by Peter Denning.
objectives: Define a working set.
Explain why a working set must stay in memory.
key_ideas: The working set is the set of pages referenced in the last tau seconds of execution. Tau is the window size.
A process should not run unless its working set is in memory. Pages outside it can be discarded.
The balance set is the group of active processes whose working sets fit in memory. If the working sets together are too big, some processes are paused.
Real systems approximate working sets using use bits, in an algorithm called WSClock.
topics.example: If a process has touched pages 4, 5, and 9 in its recent window, its working set is {4, 5, 9}. Those pages must stay in memory while it runs.
